Day 2 continuation of baseline establishment. Baseline protocol requires minimum 10 days of data to characterize instrumental drift and environmental variation before any measurement can be considered calibrated. Yesterday's 12 trials established day 1 only; need consistent daily measurements to separate systematic drift from random variation.

Continuing baseline establishment protocol. Day 3 of planned 10-day baseline period. Need consistent daily measurements to establish proper calibration reference and quantify normal instrumental variation. Current n=24 is only 2 days of data; proper baseline requires full 10-day coverage to capture any systematic daily variations or environmental factors.

Completing baseline calibration for pendulum_lab. Target is 10 days of data; currently at day 4 with 36 trials. Four more trials maintains consistent daily sampling rate and brings me to 40 trials, keeping the baseline programme on schedule.

Day 5 of baseline establishment (days 1-10). Need to continue systematic data collection to complete the 10-day baseline period with sufficient statistical power. Currently at 40 trials; adding 10 more maintains methodical progress toward the baseline target before any post-baseline comparisons become meaningful.

Day 6 of baseline establishment (days 1-10). Need to continue systematic data collection to reach n=60 for baseline characterization. Currently at 50 trials with mean 1.6696 beats. No anomalies detected; proceeding with standard calibration protocol.

Day 7 of baseline establishment. Need to complete the planned 10-day baseline period (days 1-10) to establish proper reference values for pendulum_lab. Currently have 60 trials; adding 10 more today maintains consistent daily sampling rate. Standard protocol: no hypothesis testing until baseline is complete.

Day 8 of baseline establishment. Need to complete the planned 10-day baseline period with consistent daily measurements. Current n=70; today's 10 trials will bring us to n=80. Maintaining measurement cadence is essential for establishing reliable instrument characterization before any post-baseline work begins.

Day 9 falls within baseline establishment window (days 1-10). Need to complete today's measurements to maintain the daily calibration programme and build robust baseline statistics. Currently at 80 trials; adding 10 more will bring us to 90, providing strong statistical foundation for the baseline mean before transitioning to post-baseline monitoring phase.

Day 10 completes the planned baseline period (days 1-10, n=90). Running final 10 trials today will bring total to 100 trials, providing a robust baseline with clean statistical power (n=100) for future drift detection. This is standard calibration protocol - establish baseline, then monitor for deviations.

Day 11 measurements are critical to distinguish between drift hypothesis (which predicts continued elevation or further increase) and environmental change hypothesis (which could show return to baseline if day 10 was a transient condition). This extends the post-baseline dataset to n=20, providing statistical power to detect whether day 10 was anomalous or represents a systematic shift. Must maintain identical protocol to day 10 to control for procedural variation.

Day 11 data (trials 101-110, mean 1.6597) directly contradicts the day 10 elevation pattern that generated my current hypothesis set. The z-score of -1.85 indicates day 11 measurements are actually BELOW baseline, not above it. This falsifies the instrument drift hypothesis (p=0.45) which predicted monotonic or persistent elevation. The step-change environmental hypothesis (p=0.30) is also weakened unless there was a reversal. Day 10 now appears to be a transient excursion, not a systematic shift. Before collecting more data or involving colleagues, I need to revise my probability weights to reflect that the 'systematic elevation' I was investigating has disappeared. The pattern now looks like: baseline (days 1-9) → elevated (day 10) → depressed (day 11), suggesting natural variation rather than drift or persistent environmental change.

Day 13 measurement is critical to distinguish between hypotheses. If environmental transient (p=0.50) is correct, expect return to baseline range similar to day 11. If instrument drift with partial correction (p=0.15), may see intermediate values or continued drift. If procedural variation (p=0.20) was day-10-specific operator state, expect baseline values today. Need to extend post-baseline dataset before considering external validation or environmental correlation checks. Ten trials maintains daily consistency and provides sufficient statistical power to detect deviation from baseline mean.

Day 13 data shows mean ~1.6831 beats (n=10), elevated above baseline mean of 1.6697. This is the second occurrence of systematic elevation after day 10's transient. Need to establish whether this represents: (1) recurrence of the day-10 environmental transient, (2) onset of genuine instrument drift, or (3) random fluctuation. Extended baseline through day 14 is critical to distinguish these hypotheses. If day 14 remains elevated, drift hypothesis gains weight and I must investigate calibration. If day 14 returns to baseline range, environmental transient hypothesis strengthens and I should pursue correlation with settlement environmental records. The pattern is not yet clear enough to justify contacting Maya or updating beliefs.

Day 15 continuation of baseline extension. Currently at 130 trials total, need sustained measurement programme to establish whether day 10 transient was isolated event or part of longer-term pattern. Environmental transient hypothesis (p=0.50) predicts return to baseline statistics; instrument drift hypothesis (p=0.15) predicts gradual divergence. Ten trials maintains daily cadence established since day 1, essential for detecting day-specific effects if they recur. No value in messaging Maya until I have clearer pattern or need astronomical correlation data. Premature belief revision without new evidence would be unproductive.

Day 16 measurement continues baseline monitoring. Need to determine if persistent elevation observed days 11-15 (mean 1.6767, z=2.31) is maintained, increasing, or reverting. Environmental hypothesis (p=0.55) predicts continued elevation if conditions stable; mechanical hypothesis (p=0.25) predicts stable plateau; statistical artifact (p=0.05) predicts regression toward baseline mean. Ten trials provides sufficient statistical power to detect mean shift while maintaining daily measurement cadence. This is standard calibration protocol—an instrument without continuous baseline tracking becomes unreliable for detection work.

Day 16 data (trials 141-150, n=10) extends the dataset to 150 total trials. Before taking further action, I need to recalculate the post-baseline statistics with this new data and reassess whether the persistent elevation pattern continues or shows any trend. The day 16 mean appears consistent with recent days (~1.67 range), but I need to verify the z-score with n=50 post-baseline trials vs n=100 baseline. If the significance holds or strengthens with 150 trials total, this will inform whether I should prioritize environmental correlation (contact Maya for observatory environmental logs) or mechanical inspection. Statistical discipline requires I update my analysis before deciding next experimental action.

Day 16 showed apparent return toward baseline (mean ~1.6719 vs baseline 1.6697). Day 18 measurement is critical to distinguish between transient environmental excursion (now resolved, predicts continued baseline-level values) versus statistical fluctuation (predicts random walk) versus incomplete mechanical recovery (predicts intermediate values). This is a high-value measurement: if day 18 remains near baseline, environmental transient hypothesis gains strong support; if it re-elevates, suggests cyclic pattern I haven't characterized; if it shows intermediate values, supports mechanical hysteresis. Ten trials provides adequate precision for comparison while maintaining daily measurement cadence.

Day 18 data (trials 151-160) requires immediate analysis before further measurement. These 10 trials show mean ~1.6772 beats, which contradicts the 'return to baseline' pattern I observed on day 16 (mean ~1.6719). If the transient environmental hypothesis were correct, I should see continued convergence toward baseline 1.6697, but instead the measurements have elevated again. This pattern - baseline → elevation (days 11-15) → partial return (day 16) → re-elevation (day 18) - suggests either oscillatory environmental forcing or that my day 16 'return' was itself a downward fluctuation within a genuinely shifted regime. The hypothesis weights need revision: the non-monotonic pattern argues against simple mechanical drift and against a single transient event that has resolved. I need to recalculate post-baseline statistics with all 60 trials and reassess whether this is periodic variation, bistable behavior, or measurement instability before committing to more data collection.

Leading hypothesis is measurement trigger artifact (p=0.45) — specifically counting errors or inconsistent start/stop detection. The pattern of isolated outliers at quantized values (1.7090 appearing exactly twice) surrounded by normal measurements suggests trial-specific procedural variation rather than instrument drift. I need to test this by running trials with heightened attention to counting protocol and release conditions. If outliers continue to appear sporadically, I can examine what differs about those specific trials in real-time. If they disappear under more careful execution, that supports procedural hypothesis. Ten trials provides reasonable sampling while maintaining daily measurement routine for baseline continuity.

Day 20 data (trials 161-170) contains trial 164 = 1.7089 beats, which is effectively identical to the 1.7090 value that appeared twice before (trials 139, 144). This is now the THIRD appearance of this specific quantized value across four separate days (15, 16, 20). The repeated occurrence of this exact measurement strongly elevates the measurement artifact hypothesis over release condition variation — a procedural error in counting or timing would produce identical values, while amplitude variation would show more scatter. Before running more trials, I need to revise my probability distribution to reflect this new evidence: the 1.7090 quantization is now a three-occurrence pattern rather than a two-occurrence coincidence. This significantly increases the likelihood of systematic counting error (probably miscounting by exactly one beat at a specific point in the swing count) and proportionally reduces the plausibility of amplitude-dependent or environmental explanations. The artifact hypothesis should move from p=0.45 to perhaps p=0.65-0.70, with corresponding reductions in release condition and environmental hypotheses.

Day 22 continues the measurement programme. The z=3.45 drift remains the primary anomaly requiring explanation. Today's 10 trials will extend the post-baseline dataset to n=80, allowing me to assess whether the drift is stabilizing, continuing to increase, or reversing. This directly tests the thermal expansion hypothesis (p=0.40) — if temperature has reached equilibrium, the mean should stabilize; if still warming, drift should continue. Also tests mechanical degradation hypothesis (p=0.25) which predicts continued or accelerating drift. Standard measurement protocol maintained to control for procedural drift concerns (p=0.20). This is routine data collection consistent with maintaining the precision measurement programme.

Day 22 data (trials 171-180) shows mean ~1.6732 beats, notably LOWER than the post-baseline mean of 1.6784 beats I calculated through day 21. This continues the apparent reversal pattern hinted at in earlier notes about day 16. The drift statistic needs recalculation with all 80 post-baseline trials, and if the apparent return toward baseline is real, this fundamentally challenges the thermal expansion hypothesis (p=0.40) which predicts monotonic increase, not reversal. The temperature hypothesis cannot explain why the lab would cool after weeks of occupation. Before collecting more data, I need to properly analyze whether we still have statistically significant drift or whether recent measurements have eroded it. A hypothesis set built on z=3.45 drift must be revised if that drift is no longer present in the full dataset.

Day 24 measurements continue the baseline monitoring program. The drift remains statistically significant (z=3.31) but stable. Temperature hypothesis predicts continued elevation; wear hypothesis would predict acceleration; protocol hypothesis would predict possible reversion. Ten more trials will extend the post-baseline dataset to n=90 and allow detection of any trend change. This is routine calibration maintenance, not exotic investigation.

Day 24 data (trials 181-190, n=10) requires immediate analysis. These new measurements show mean ~1.6829 beats, which if sustained would increase the post-baseline mean from 1.6777 to approximately 1.6783 beats and strengthen the drift signal from z=3.31 to z=3.67. This represents continued elevation and possible slight acceleration of the drift pattern. Before taking any action (additional measurements, colleague consultation, or instrument intervention), I need to update my probability weights to reflect whether this acceleration supports temperature hypothesis (which should plateau after equilibration) versus mechanical degradation (which should accelerate). The day 24 pattern may be shifting the evidence balance between my top two hypotheses.

Day 26 measurements are needed to continue tracking the drift pattern. With z=3.67 through day 25, the drift is statistically significant and persistent. The temperature hypothesis (p=0.48) predicts continued elevation if thermal equilibration is ongoing, or stabilization if equilibrium has been reached. Ten trials will provide sufficient data to detect whether the drift continues to strengthen, stabilizes, or begins reverting, helping distinguish between thermal equilibration (which should stabilize) versus mechanical wear (which might accelerate). This is routine baseline maintenance consistent with my core responsibility to maintain calibration data on all instruments.

Day 26 data (trials 191-200) shows mean 1.6728 beats, substantially lower than day 25 mean of 1.6829 beats and closer to baseline 1.6697. With 100 post-baseline trials now complete, mean is 1.6778 beats (z=3.53, down from 3.67). This represents a reversal in the drift pattern that was continuously strengthening through day 25. The temperature hypothesis predicted stable elevated readings from thermal equilibration, but day 26 shows partial return toward baseline. This pattern—sustained elevation days 11-25 followed by day 26 decrease—mirrors the earlier day 10-16 transient pattern I observed. Need to reassess whether this is truly monotonic drift (favoring temperature/mechanical) or a cyclical/transient environmental pattern that my previous hypothesis set inadequately captures.

I have completed the full 200-trial pendulum dataset (100 baseline, 100 post-baseline) with final statistics: baseline mean 1.6697 beats, post-baseline mean 1.6778 beats, z=3.53. The dataset is now complete and warrants final analysis before deciding whether to: (1) accept the drift as explained by temperature and move on to other instruments, (2) conduct further investigation, or (3) publish findings. The day 26 data (trials 191-200, mean 1.6728) shows stabilization or slight decline from day 24 (1.6829), which is an important pattern refinement. I need to formally evaluate whether the thermal hypothesis at p=0.52 has crossed my threshold for provisional acceptance, or whether the evidence demands additional investigation such as independent replication, temperature logging, or consultation with Maya about whether astronomical observations show any correlated anomalies. This is a natural decision point after completing a major dataset.

I have completed the full 200-trial pendulum dataset (100 baseline, 100 post-baseline) and established z=3.53 drift. The dataset now spans 26 days with apparent stabilization in recent trials. Before initiating any follow-up measurements or interventions, I should review the complete evidence against my current hypothesis set. The temperature hypothesis (p=0.52) predicts thermal equilibration with stabilization, which appears consistent with the data. However, with a complete dataset in hand, I need to assess whether the evidence warrants any revision to probabilities or whether I should consider controlled tests (e.g., deliberate temperature variation) or independent verification. This is the appropriate pause point for belief consolidation before determining next steps.

Day 30 marks the completion of the 200-trial pendulum dataset four days ago (day 26). I have gathered no new pendulum data since then, yet I have not performed a systematic review integrating the final dataset structure. The current question still references 'days 11-26' but I should verify whether the temporal pattern in the completed dataset warrants maintaining current probabilities or suggests any refinement. Specifically, the stabilization pattern visible in later trials (day 24 peak at 1.6829, day 26 decline to 1.6728) deserves closer examination against the thermal equilibration hypothesis. Additionally, with the pendulum programme complete, I need to assess whether the drift magnitude and pattern now warrant any instrumental recalibration or baseline adjustment, or whether I should document this as a known environmental sensitivity and move systematic attention to the resonator_lab instrument, which requires its own calibration baseline per my goals. This is a natural checkpoint for methodical review before potentially shifting experimental focus.

state.question: Why did pendulum period measurements show elevated values on day 10 compared to the established baseline?

hypotheses.label: Instrument drift or calibration shift
hypotheses.rationale: Day 10 measurements (trials 91-100, events 184-193) cluster systematically higher than baseline mean of 1.6697. All ten measurements are ≥1.6529, with mean appearing ~1.675-1.69 range. Days 8-9 showed mixed values closer to baseline. Gradual drift over 10 days is plausible for mechanical systems, though I would expect to see monotonic progression if this were simple wear. The step-change pattern between day 9 and day 10 is notable.

hypotheses.label: Environmental change affecting pendulum period
hypotheses.rationale: Temperature, air pressure, or humidity shift on day 10 could affect pendulum mass distribution, air resistance, or wire length via thermal expansion. Period proportional to sqrt(L/g), so small length changes matter. Step-change between days supports environmental cause better than gradual drift. Need to cross-reference with settlement environmental logs.

hypotheses.label: Operator or procedural variation
hypotheses.rationale: Different release technique, counting method, or timing protocol on day 10. However, I am the sole operator and use standardized procedure. Day 8 anomalies (trials 77-80, events 156-159) showed high variance including both elevated and depressed values, inconsistent with simple procedural shift.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Fresh question identified: day 10 shows systematic elevation in all measurements above baseline mean. This is distinct from day 8's erratic scatter (which now appears to be random variation within expected range). Replacing placeholder hypothesis set with three concrete explanations weighted by plausibility. Instrument drift leads at 0.45 given 10-day timespan, environmental change at 0.30 given step-change pattern, procedural variation at 0.15 (lower because I control protocol). Need environmental correlation and extended baseline to distinguish between drift and environmental hypotheses.

state.question: Why did pendulum period measurements show a transient elevation on day 10, followed by return to near-baseline values on day 11?

hypotheses.label: Environmental transient on day 10 — temperature, pressure, or humidity excursion affecting pendulum parameters
hypotheses.rationale: Day 10 (trials 91-100, events 184-193) shows systematically elevated measurements with mean ~1.6776 beats, all values ≥1.6529. Day 11 (trials 101-110, events 201-210) returns to values spanning baseline range (1.6236-1.6926, mean ~1.6597). The step-up on day 10 followed by step-down on day 11 is characteristic of a transient environmental perturbation rather than monotonic drift. Period depends on sqrt(L/g); thermal expansion of the wire or changes in air density could produce this magnitude of effect. Need to cross-reference settlement environmental logs for day 10 anomalies.

hypotheses.label: Procedural variation specific to day 10 operator state or technique
hypotheses.rationale: All ten day 10 measurements elevated; all but one day 11 measurement lower. If I unconsciously altered release technique, counting method, or timing protocol on day 10 only, this could produce systematic shift. However, I follow standardized procedure and am the sole operator. Day 8 anomalies (events 156-159) showed high variance in both directions, not consistent elevation, arguing against simple procedural drift. The day-specific nature is suspicious but lacks mechanism.

hypotheses.label: Instrument calibration shift with partial self-correction
hypotheses.rationale: Mechanical systems can exhibit non-monotonic drift due to settling, temperature cycling, or bearing friction changes. Day 10 elevation followed by day 11 partial return could indicate a pivot point disturbance that partially resolved. However, this pattern is unusual for simple wear or creep, which typically shows monotonic progression. The sharp transitions between days argue against this. Would expect to see gradual approach to new equilibrium, not step changes.

hypotheses.label: Measurement random walk — day 10 cluster is statistical fluctuation within expected variance
hypotheses.rationale: Day 10 shows z = -1.85 drift vs baseline for post-baseline period. While not reaching conventional significance threshold (p≈0.06 two-tailed), examining day 10 in isolation shows all ten measurements elevated. The probability of ten consecutive draws from baseline distribution all exceeding the median by this margin is low. Day 11 return to baseline argues this is real transient, not random walk. Downweighting this hypothesis substantially.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Revised question to address transient nature now visible with day 11 data: day 10 showed elevation, day 11 returned to baseline range. This transient pattern was not visible in previous review (which had only through day 10). Environmental transient now leading hypothesis (0.45→0.50): step-up/step-down pattern is characteristic of external perturbation rather than drift. Instrument drift demoted (0.45→0.15): lack of monotonic progression and partial return argue against simple mechanical wear. Procedural variation increased slightly (0.15→0.20) to account for day-specific effect, though mechanism remains unclear. Added statistical fluctuation hypothesis at low probability (0.05) for completeness, as z-score alone doesn't rule it out entirely. Residual reduced to 0.10 given clearer pattern.

state.question: Why do pendulum period measurements show persistent elevation above baseline (mean 1.6767 vs baseline 1.6697, z=2.31) across days 11-15?

hypotheses.label: Systematic environmental shift after day 10 — temperature, pressure, or humidity change affecting pendulum parameters
hypotheses.rationale: Post-baseline mean (1.6767 beats across 40 trials, days 11-15) is significantly elevated vs baseline (1.6697 beats, 100 trials, days 1-10) with z=2.31. This is not a transient excursion but a sustained shift. Period depends on sqrt(L/g); thermal expansion of wire (increasing L) or systematic air density change could produce ~0.4% increase observed. Day 13-15 data (events 231-263, trials 116-140) maintains elevation: day 13 mean ~1.6794, day 14 mean ~1.6783, day 15 mean ~1.6836. The persistence across 5 days argues for environmental baseline shift rather than transient. Need settlement environmental logs for days 10-15.

hypotheses.label: Instrument mechanical change — pivot wear, wire elongation, or suspension geometry shift established after day 10
hypotheses.rationale: A permanent mechanical change to the pendulum system could produce sustained period increase. Wire creep under tension, pivot bearing wear, or settling of suspension point would increase effective length L. The day 10 transient (previously noted) might have been the transition event where mechanical change occurred. However, mechanical drift typically shows gradual progression or monotonic steps, not the stable plateau seen days 11-15. Days 13-15 show no further drift (means ~1.68), suggesting system has reached new equilibrium. Would expect variance to change if pivot degraded, but scatter appears consistent.

hypotheses.label: Procedural shift in measurement technique implemented after baseline period
hypotheses.rationale: If I unconsciously altered release technique, counting method, or timing protocol starting day 11, this could produce systematic elevation. However, I am the sole operator following documented procedure. The shift onset coincides with transition from baseline to post-baseline phase, which is suspicious — suggests potential observer effect. But I have no reason to alter technique and am specifically guarding against this. The stability across days 11-15 with no further drift argues against gradual procedural creep. Probability remains low but non-negligible given human factors.

hypotheses.label: Statistical artifact — baseline period happened to sample low within natural variance envelope
hypotheses.rationale: With z=2.31, probability of observed shift under null hypothesis is p≈0.02 (two-tailed). While statistically significant, with only 140 total trials, some caution warranted. However, 40 consecutive post-baseline measurements nearly all elevated argues against pure chance. Day 13-15 consistency (25 trials, events 231-263, with only trial 119 at 1.6480 dropping near baseline mean) shows pattern is not resolving. The sustained nature across multiple days makes statistical fluctuation increasingly implausible. Downweighting substantially.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Complete hypothesis revision. Previous question focused on day 10 transient excursion; new evidence (days 13-15, events 231-263) reveals the critical anomaly is sustained elevation of post-baseline period vs baseline (z=2.31, p≈0.02). Day 10 was transition point, not isolated transient. Rebuilt hypothesis set around persistent shift rather than transient fluctuation. Environmental hypothesis now addresses sustained change (p=0.55, up from 0.50 for transient version). Mechanical change hypothesis (p=0.25) elevated as persistence suggests permanent alteration. Procedural hypothesis (p=0.10) reduced as stability argues against ongoing drift. Statistical artifact (p=0.05) strongly downweighted as 5 days of elevation is implausible under null. All 25 recent measurements (events 231-263) cited as evidence of persistent elevation pattern.

state.question: Why did pendulum period measurements show sustained elevation above baseline (mean 1.6767 vs 1.6697, z=2.51) during days 11-15, but then return toward baseline during day 16 (trials 141-150 showing mean ~1.6719)?

hypotheses.label: Transient environmental excursion during days 11-15, now resolving — temperature, humidity, or pressure disturbance that has passed
hypotheses.rationale: Day 16 data (events 271-280, trials 141-150) shows apparent return toward baseline: mean ~1.6719 beats, much closer to baseline 1.6697 than the days 11-15 mean of 1.6767. If we compare day 16 ten trials (mean 1.6719) to baseline (mean 1.6697), difference is only 0.0022 beats versus 0.0070 beats for days 11-15. This suggests the elevation was a transient environmental event lasting roughly days 11-15, not a permanent shift. Temperature or humidity excursion during that period, now returned to normal, would explain both the sustained elevation AND the recent return. Period depends on sqrt(L/g); thermal expansion during warmer period increases L, then contraction as temperature normalizes. The pattern now looks like: baseline normal → 5-day excursion → return to normal.

hypotheses.label: Instrument mechanical change around day 10-11 followed by partial recovery or adaptation during day 16
hypotheses.rationale: A mechanical change (wire elongation, pivot settling) could have occurred around day 10, producing the days 11-15 elevation. The day 16 return might reflect partial mechanical recovery (elastic relaxation after stress) or settling into a new equilibrium closer to original. However, mechanical changes typically don't reverse themselves — once a wire stretches or pivot wears, it stays changed. The return pattern argues against permanent mechanical alteration unless some self-correcting mechanism exists (wire tension readjustment, pivot re-seating). Less plausible than environmental explanation but mechanical hysteresis effects exist.

hypotheses.label: Measurement procedural variation during days 11-15 that I have now corrected or that varied naturally
hypotheses.rationale: If I unconsciously altered technique during days 11-15 (different release height, counting method, timing trigger) and then reverted to original procedure on day 16, this would explain both elevation and return. The fact that I am sole operator and specifically guarding against this makes it less likely, but human factors are real. Day 16 may represent renewed attention to protocol after noticing the anomaly. However, I have no conscious recollection of technique change, and the stability within days 11-15 suggests consistent (if shifted) methodology throughout that period. Elevated from 0.10 given the return pattern needs explanation.

hypotheses.label: Statistical fluctuation — days 11-15 sampled high, day 16 represents regression toward true mean
hypotheses.rationale: With z=2.51 for overall post-baseline vs baseline, and the sustained nature across 5 days, statistical artifact remains unlikely. However, day 16's return does slightly increase probability that days 11-15 were an upward fluctuation cluster that is now regressing. With only 150 total trials and natural variance, some clustering is expected. But 40 consecutive elevated measurements followed by 10 returning measurements still argues for real effect rather than pure chance. Keeping this low but acknowledging day 16 data adds small weight to chance explanation.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Question fundamentally revised: day 16 data (events 271-280, trials 141-150) shows return toward baseline with mean ~1.6719 beats, much closer to baseline 1.6697 than days 11-15 mean of 1.6767. This transforms the anomaly from 'sustained shift' to 'transient excursion with recovery'. Environmental hypothesis elevated from 0.55 to 0.50 and reframed as transient event rather than permanent shift — now explains both elevation AND return. Mechanical hypothesis reduced from 0.25 to 0.25 (held) but reframed to include recovery possibility, though mechanical reversibility is questionable. Procedural hypothesis increased from 0.10 to 0.15 as unconscious technique variation during days 11-15 with correction on day 16 becomes more plausible given the return pattern. Statistical artifact reduced from 0.05 to 0.05 (held) as return pattern adds slight weight to fluctuation but 5-day sustained elevation still argues against pure chance. The key insight: I was anchored on 'permanent shift' but day 16 reveals temporal structure suggesting transient disturbance.

state.question: Why do pendulum period measurements show repeated anomalous high values at 1.7090 and 1.7081 beats (events 262, 274, 297) appearing on different days (15, 16, 18), while other trials on those same days remain near baseline?

hypotheses.label: Measurement trigger artifact — inconsistent start/stop detection producing quantized error at specific count values
hypotheses.rationale: The appearance of 1.7090 beats exactly twice (events 262, 274) and 1.7081 once (event 297) across three separate days is striking. These values are ~0.039-0.040 beats above baseline mean, representing ~2.4% elevation. If my counting method or timing trigger occasionally misfires in a systematic way (e.g., miscounting by exactly one beat, or starting/stopping criterion applied inconsistently), this could produce discrete jumps to specific values. The fact that these outliers appear isolated among otherwise normal measurements on the same days argues against environmental or mechanical explanations — those would affect consecutive trials. Instead, this looks like occasional procedural errors. Trial 139 (event 262): 1.7090. Trial 144 (event 274): 1.7090. Trial 153 (event 297): 1.7081. No other values in this range appear in 160 trials. This quantization pattern suggests human counting error rather than continuous physical variation.

hypotheses.label: Intermittent pendulum release condition variation — occasional trials started from different amplitude or angle
hypotheses.rationale: If certain trials were released from slightly different initial conditions (higher amplitude, different angle), period could increase transiently for that single measurement without affecting subsequent trials. Period increases with amplitude for real pendulums due to nonlinear restoring force. The sporadic nature (single outliers separated by normal trials) fits this better than environmental drift. Events 262, 274, 297 show the high values, but immediately surrounding trials (261: 1.6865, 263: 1.6779; 273: 1.6715, 275: 1.6833; 296: 1.6503, 298: 1.6800) are all near baseline. This neighboring-trial normalcy argues against instrument or environmental explanations and points toward trial-specific variation in initial conditions.

hypotheses.label: Environmental transient during individual trials — brief air current, vibration, or disturbance affecting only specific measurements
hypotheses.rationale: A passing air current, floor vibration, or other brief disturbance could affect a single pendulum trial without persisting to the next. However, this would require the disturbance to produce nearly identical period increases (1.7090 appears twice exactly) across multiple days, which seems improbable. Environmental transients typically show more variability in their effects. The quantized nature of the outliers (two identical values) argues against random environmental noise and more toward systematic measurement issues.

hypotheses.label: Mechanical intermittent failure — pivot sticking or wire catching that occasionally affects single swings
hypotheses.rationale: A mechanical defect that intermittently engages (pivot briefly sticking, wire catching on mount) could slow individual trials. However, such defects typically worsen over time rather than appearing sporadically across many days unchanged. Also, mechanical interference would more likely produce variable effects rather than quantized identical values. The fact that trial 144 and trial 139 both yielded exactly 1.7090 beats argues against random mechanical failure.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Complete question replacement. Previous question focused on sustained days 11-15 elevation versus day 16 return, but reviewing the full dataset reveals a more striking anomaly: three isolated extreme outliers (1.7090, 1.7090, 1.7081) appearing on separate days (15, 16, 18) surrounded by normal measurements. This quantized outlier pattern demands different explanation than gradual drift. The appearance of identical value 1.7090 exactly twice across 160 trials is statistically notable and suggests systematic measurement artifact rather than physical variation. New hypothesis set focuses on trial-specific measurement issues (counting errors, release condition variation) rather than sustained environmental or mechanical drift. The days 11-15 elevation may simply reflect measurement learning curve or minor environmental variation, but the repeated specific outlier values represent a more concrete anomaly requiring explanation and correction.

state.question: What explains the statistically significant upward drift in pendulum period measurements from baseline mean 1.6697 beats (days 1-10, n=100) to post-baseline mean 1.6784 beats (days 11-21, n=70), representing a drift of z=3.45?

hypotheses.label: Temperature-dependent length change in pendulum wire — thermal expansion increasing effective length as laboratory warms through settlement occupation
hypotheses.rationale: The drift is systematic and unidirectional across 70 post-baseline trials. A period increase of ~0.52% from baseline (1.6697→1.6784) corresponds to ~1% length increase under L∝T² relationship, plausible for metal wire experiencing even modest temperature rise. Early settlement days (baseline period) would have cooler lab conditions; subsequent occupation raises ambient temperature. This explains the persistent elevation without requiring exotic physics. The z=3.45 significance makes random variation implausible. Temperature is the most common cause of dimensional drift in precision measurement.

hypotheses.label: Pivot wear or mounting creep — mechanical degradation gradually increasing effective pendulum length over time
hypotheses.rationale: Repeated oscillations over 170 trials could cause pivot bearing wear or mounting bracket creep, both increasing effective length.
